translations.idiomatic: His father Zao held the post of commissioner of waterways.

sentences.zh: 邈姿性端雅，勤行勵學，博涉多聞，以慎密自居。

translations.literal: Miao’s bearing was proper and refined; he labored at conduct and spurred himself in study, read widely and heard much, and prided himself on discretion and reticence.
translations.idiomatic: Xu Miao was dignified, industrious, widely read, and guarded his tongue.

sentences.zh: 少與鄉人臧壽齊名，下帷讀書，不遊城邑。

translations.literal: In youth he shared fame with his townsman Zang Shou; he let down the curtain to read and did not roam the cities.
translations.idiomatic: As a young man he matched the local reputation of Zang Shou, studied behind closed doors, and avoided urban distractions.

sentences.zh: 及孝武帝始覽典籍，招延儒學之士，邈既東州儒素，太傅謝安舉以應選。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xiaowu first turned to the classical corpus and summoned Ru scholars, Miao, already a plain scholar of the eastern quarter, was recommended by Grand Tutor Xie An for selection.
translations.idiomatic: Once Emperor Xiaowu began patronizing classics, Grand Tutor Xie An nominated the respected eastern scholar Xu Miao.

sentences.zh: 年四十四，始補中書舍人，在西省侍帝。

translations.literal: At forty-four he was first appointed secretariat gentleman and attended the emperor in the Western Office.
translations.idiomatic: At forty-four he entered office as secretariat gentleman, serving in the Western Bureau beside the throne.

sentences.zh: 雖不口傳章句，然開釋文義，標明指趣，撰正五經音訓，學者宗之。

translations.literal: Although he did not orally transmit chapter-and-verse glosses, in opening and explaining literary meaning and marking out the points of interest he corrected the phonological glosses on the five classics, and students took him as their authority.
translations.idiomatic: He seldom lectured line by line, yet his explanations of meaning and his corrected pronunciations for the five classics became the standard for scholars.

sentences.zh: 遷散騎常侍，猶處西省，前後十年，每被顧問，輒有獻替，多所匡益，甚見寵待。

translations.literal: He was promoted cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, still stationed in the Western Office; for ten years before and after, whenever questioned in audience he offered replacements and improvements, correcting and benefiting much, and was greatly favored.
translations.idiomatic: As cavalier attendant he remained in the Western Office a decade, and each imperial consultation brought sound emendations that earned deep trust.

sentences.zh: 帝宴集酣樂之後，好為手詔詩章以賜侍臣，或文詞率爾，所言穢雜，邈每應時收斂，還省刊削，皆使可觀，經帝重覽，然後出之。

translations.literal: After feasts when the emperor was drunk and merry, he liked to draft by hand poems and edicts to give attendant ministers; sometimes the wording was hasty and the content coarse, but Miao each time gathered them in, returned to office to edit and cut, making them presentable, and only after the emperor had reviewed them again would they be issued.
translations.idiomatic: When feasts left the sovereign tipsy, his handwritten poems and orders could be crude; Xu Miao collected them, polished the language at his desk, and held them until the emperor approved a clean text.

sentences.zh: 是時侍臣被詔者，或宣揚之，故時議以此多邈。

translations.literal: At that time attendants who received such edicts sometimes publicized them, so contemporary opinion on this account favored Miao.
translations.idiomatic: Recipients sometimes leaked those drafts, which made court opinion esteem Xu Miao all the more.

sentences.zh: 及謝安薨，論者或有異同，邈固勸中書令王獻之奏加殊禮，仍崇進謝石為尚書令，玄為徐州。

translations.literal: When Xie An died, debaters were divided; Miao firmly urged Secretariat Director Wang Xianzhi to memorialize for special rites, and still promoted Xie Shi to imperial secretary and Xie Xuan to governor of Xuzhou.
translations.idiomatic: After Xie An’s death opinion split; Xu Miao pressed Wang Xianzhi to grant extraordinary honors and helped advance Xie Shi and Xie Xuan to key posts.

sentences.zh: 邈轉祠部郎，上南北郊宗廟迭毀禮，皆有證據。

translations.literal: Miao was transferred to director of the sacrifices bureau and submitted memorials on the rotating destruction of suburban and ancestral shrines, each with supporting evidence.
translations.idiomatic: As director of sacrifices he memorialized on the cycling removal of spirit tablets at suburban and temple rites, citing chapter and verse.

sentences.zh: 豫章太守范甯欲遣十五議曹下屬城采求風政，並使假還，訊問官長得失。

translations.literal: Governor of Yuzhang Fan Ning wished to dispatch fifteen deliberation clerks to subordinate counties to collect information on customs and administration, and also grant them leave to return and report what they had heard of officials’ merits and faults.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Ning of Yuzhang planned to send fifteen staff investigators into his counties to gauge local government, then recall them to report on magistrates.

sentences.zh: 邈與寧書曰：

translations.literal: Miao wrote Ning a letter saying:
translations.idiomatic: Xu Miao wrote to Fan Ning:

sentences.zh: 知足下遣十五議曹各之一縣，又吏假歸，白所聞見，誠是足下留意百姓，故廣其視聽。

translations.literal: I know that you have sent fifteen deliberation clerks each to a county, and that clerks on leave return to tell what they have seen and heard—this truly shows you mind the common people and therefore widen your sight and hearing.
translations.idiomatic: You have posted fifteen advisers to the counties and debrief returning clerks—clearly you care for the people and want broader intelligence.

sentences.zh: 吾謂勸導以實不以文，十五議曹欲何所敷宣邪？

translations.literal: I say guidance should rely on substance, not display—what do fifteen deliberation clerks intend to proclaim?
translations.idiomatic: Yet honest leadership rests on deeds, not spectacle—what message will those fifteen envoys preach?

sentences.zh: 庶事辭訟，足下聽斷允塞，則物理足矣。

translations.literal: For the myriad affairs of lawsuits, if your listening and judgments are fair and thorough, then the pattern of things is sufficient.
translations.idiomatic: If you hear cases with consistent justice, the realm’s business is already well served.

sentences.zh: 上有理務之心，則物理足矣。

translations.literal: When the superior has a mind to order affairs, then the pattern of things is sufficient.
translations.idiomatic: When the chief magistrate truly governs, principle takes care of itself.

sentences.zh: 上有理務之心，則下之求理者至矣。

translations.literal: When the superior has a mind to order affairs, then those below who seek good order will arrive.
translations.idiomatic: When you show resolve to administer, capable men will come forward on their own.

sentences.zh: 日昃省覽，庶事無滯，則吏慎其負而入聽不惑，豈須邑至里詣，飾其遊聲哉！

translations.literal: If at sunset you review business so that nothing stalls, then clerks will fear dereliction and those who plead will not be misled—why must every hamlet be visited to polish a traveling reputation!
translations.idiomatic: Review dossiers daily so work does not pile up; clerks will then fear negligence and litigants see clearly—there is no need to tour every lane burnishing a false reputation.

sentences.zh: 非徒不足致益，乃是蠶漁之所資，又不可縱小吏為耳目也。

translations.literal: Not only will this fail to bring benefit—it supplies material for silkworm-fish style predation—and you cannot let petty clerks serve as eyes and ears either.
translations.idiomatic: Such busywork invites extortion and trains informers; lowly clerks must not become your spies.

sentences.zh: 豈有善人君子而幹非其事，多所告白者乎！

translations.literal: How could there be good men and gentlemen who meddle in what is not their business and carry tale after tale!
translations.idiomatic: What true gentleman pries into others’ duties and peddles gossip?

sentences.zh: 君子之心，誰毀誰譽？

translations.literal: In the heart of the gentleman, whom does he malign, whom does he praise?
translations.idiomatic: The Analects asks whom the noble man praises or blames—he does neither lightly.

sentences.zh: 如有所譽，必由歷試；

translations.literal: If there is praise, it must follow tested service;
translations.idiomatic: Any praise must rest on proven performance;

sentences.zh: 如有所毀，必以著明。

translations.literal: if there is blame, it must be because something is manifestly clear.
translations.idiomatic: any blame must rest on clear evidence.

sentences.zh: 托社之鼠，政之其害。

translations.literal: The rat that clings to the altar of the soil god is a harm to government.
translations.idiomatic: Rats hiding under the state altar—classic parasites of good rule.

sentences.zh: 自古以來，欲為左右耳目者，無非小人，皆先因小忠而成其大不忠，先藉小信而成其大不信，遂使君子道消，善人輿屍，前史所書，可為深鑒。

translations.literal: From antiquity, those who wished to be left and right ears and eyes have without exception been petty men; they all first borrow small loyalty to accomplish great disloyalty, first rely on small trustworthiness to accomplish great untrustworthiness, and thereby cause the way of gentlemen to wane and good men to perish in carts of shame—what the histories record should be a deep mirror.
translations.idiomatic: History shows that rulers who recruit petty informants breed great treason from small favors—virtue fades and worthies die in disgrace; past annals are warning enough.

sentences.zh: 足下選綱紀必得國士，足以攝諸曹；

translations.literal: If in choosing your supervisory officials you are sure to obtain men of the state, they will suffice to control the various bureaus;
translations.idiomatic: Pick national-caliber overseers and they will hold every department in line;

sentences.zh: 諸曹皆是良吏，則足以掌文案；

translations.literal: if the bureaus are all good clerks, they will suffice to manage documents;
translations.idiomatic: fill those desks with honest clerks and paperwork stays sound;

sentences.zh: 又擇公方之人以為監司，則清濁能否，與事而明。

translations.literal: further choose upright men as inspectors, then purity and turbidity, ability and inability, will be clear as each task unfolds.
translations.idiomatic: add impartial inspectors and merit becomes obvious case by case.

sentences.zh: 足下但平心居宗，何取於耳目哉！

translations.literal: You need only keep a level heart and uphold the fundamental—why borrow eyes and ears!
translations.idiomatic: Keep a calm center and you need no network of spies.

sentences.zh: 昔明德馬後未嘗顧與左右言，可謂遠識，況大丈夫而不能免此乎！

translations.literal: Long ago the illustrious Empress Ma never glanced sideways to whisper with attendants—such may be called far-sighted knowledge; how much more should a great man not fall into this!
translations.idiomatic: Empress Ma of Han refused palace whispers—far-sighted indeed; surely a statesman can shun petty eavesdroppers.

sentences.zh: 遷中書侍郎，專掌綸詔，帝甚親昵之。

translations.literal: He was promoted gentleman of the secretariat, exclusively in charge of silken edicts, and the emperor was very intimate with him.
translations.idiomatic: Raised to secretariat gentleman, he drafted edicts alone and stood among the sovereign’s closest advisers.

sentences.zh: 初，范寧與邈皆為帝所任使，共補朝廷之闕。

translations.literal: At first Fan Ning and Miao were both employed by the emperor to remedy court shortcomings.
translations.idiomatic: Early on Fan Ning and Xu Miao together repaired institutional gaps for the throne.

sentences.zh: 甯才素高而措心正直，遂為王國寶所讒，出守遠郡。

translations.literal: Ning’s talent was naturally high but his mind set on integrity, so he was slandered by Wang Guobao and sent out to guard a distant commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Ning’s brilliance and blunt honesty drew Wang Guobao’s malice and exile to a remote post.

sentences.zh: 邈孤宦易危，而無敢排強族，乃為自安之計。

translations.literal: Miao, a lone official in a perilous position, dared not confront powerful clans, and therefore planned for his own security.
translations.idiomatic: Xu Miao, isolated and vulnerable, avoided challenging great families and schemed for self-preservation.

sentences.zh: 會帝頗疏會稽王道子，邈欲和協之，因從容言於帝曰：「昔淮南、齊王，漢晉成戒。

translations.literal: When it happened that the emperor was rather estranged from Prince Kuaiji, Sima Daozi, Miao wished to harmonize them, and therefore said at his ease to the emperor: "In olden days the kings of Huainan and Qi were warnings to Han and Jin.
translations.idiomatic: Noting tension between the emperor and Prince Kuaiji, Sima Daozi, Xu Miao sought reconciliation: "The princes of Huainan and Qi taught Han and Jin hard lessons.

sentences.zh: 會稽王雖有酣媟之累，而奉上純一，宜加弘貸，消散紛議，外為國家之計，內慰太后之心。

translations.literal: The Prince of Kuaiji, though he has the blemish of drunken license, in serving superiors is utterly single-minded; you ought to treat him with generous indulgence, scatter contentious talk, outwardly plan for the state, inwardly comfort the empress dowager’s heart."
translations.idiomatic: Kuaiji may drink too much, yet his loyalty is pure—indulge him, silence backbiting, serve the realm abroad and the empress dowager at home."

sentences.zh: 」帝納焉。

translations.literal: The emperor accepted this.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor agreed.

sentences.zh: 邈嘗詣東府，遇眾賓沈湎，引滿喧嘩。

translations.literal: Miao once went to the Eastern Office and encountered a crowd of guests sunk in drink, brimming cups and shouting.
translations.idiomatic: Visiting Daozi’s eastern bureau, he found a roaring, drunken party.

sentences.zh: 道子曰：「君時有暢不？

translations.literal: Daozi said, "Do you ever feel really uninhibited?"
translations.idiomatic: Daozi asked, "Don’t you ever let yourself go?"

sentences.zh: 」邈對曰：「邈陋巷書生，惟以節儉清修為暢耳。

translations.literal: Miao replied, "Miao is a bookish fellow from a mean lane; for uninhibited feeling I have only frugality and clean cultivation."
translations.idiomatic: Xu Miao answered, "I am a poor scholar—my idea of abandon is thrift and moral discipline."

sentences.zh: 」道子以邈業尚道素，笑而不以為忤也。

translations.literal: Daozi, because Miao’s undertakings honored the plain Way, laughed and did not take it as offense.
translations.idiomatic: Daozi, knowing Xu Miao’s austere values, laughed without taking offense.

sentences.zh: 道子將用為吏部郎，邈以波競成俗，非己所能節制，苦辭乃止。

translations.literal: Daozi was about to employ him as director of the ministry of personnel, but Miao, because factional competition had become custom, felt it was not something he could control, and with bitter pleading stopped it.
translations.idiomatic: Daozi meant to name him personnel director; Xu Miao, seeing appointment wars as beyond his control, begged off until the idea died.

sentences.zh: 時皇太子尚幼，帝甚鐘心，文武之選皆一時之後。

translations.literal: At that time the crown prince was still young, and the emperor doted on him; selections for civil and military posts were all the foremost men of the age.
translations.idiomatic: The crown prince was a child, deeply cherished; civil and military appointments around him were the day’s best talent.

sentences.zh: 以邈為前衛率，領本郡大中正，授太子經。

translations.literal: He appointed Miao commandant of the forward guard, concurrently chief assessor for his home commandery, and charged him to instruct the heir in the classics.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor named Xu Miao forward-guard commandant, chief assessor for his native commandery, and tutor in the classics to the heir.

sentences.zh: 帝謂邈曰：「雖未敕以師禮相待，然不以博士相遇也。

translations.literal: The emperor told Miao: "Although I have not ordered that you be treated with the rites due a teacher, neither will I receive you as a mere erudite."
translations.idiomatic: "I may not give you full master’s rites," said the emperor, "but you are no ordinary erudite either."

sentences.zh: 」古之帝王，受經必敬，自魏晉以來，多使微人教授，號為博士，不復尊以為師，故帝有云。

translations.literal: Ancient emperors who received the classics invariably showed respect; from Wei and Jin onward they mostly had humble men instruct, titled erudite, and no longer honored them as teachers—therefore the emperor had these words.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient rulers honored their classicists; since Wei and Jin, low-born "erudites" lost that dignity—hence the emperor’s remark.

sentences.zh: 邈雖在東宮，猶朝夕入見，參綜朝政，修飾文詔，拾遺補闕，劬勞左右。

translations.literal: Although Miao was in the Eastern Palace, he still morning and evening entered to be seen, participated in synthesizing court governance, polished literary edicts, picked up oversights and supplied omissions, and toiled at the ruler’s side.
translations.idiomatic: Even while attached to the heir’s household he attended court daily, helped steer policy, edited state papers, and filled gaps beside the throne.

sentences.zh: 帝嘉其謹密，方之于金霍，有托重之意，將進顯位，未及行而帝暴崩。

translations.literal: The emperor praised his careful discretion, comparing him to Jin Midi and Huo Guang, with intentions of entrusting heavy responsibility; he was about to advance him to a conspicuous post, but before it could be carried out the emperor suddenly collapsed.
translations.idiomatic: The sovereign likened his prudence to Jin Midi and Huo Guang and planned higher office—then died abruptly.

sentences.zh: 安帝即位，拜驍騎將軍。

translations.literal: When Emperor An ascended the throne, Miao was appointed general of fierce cavalry.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor An named him general of fierce cavalry.

sentences.zh: 隆安元年，遭父憂。

translations.literal: In the first year of Longan he suffered his father’s mourning.
translations.idiomatic: In Longan year one he entered mourning for his father.

sentences.zh: 邈先疾患，因哀毀增篤，不逾年而卒，年五十四，州里傷悼，識者悲之。

translations.literal: Miao had already been ill; with grief and emaciation it grew severe, and before a year had passed he died, aged fifty-four; the district mourned him, and those who knew him grieved.
translations.idiomatic: Already sick, grief broke him; within the year he died at fifty-four, mourned locally and by every friend.

sentences.zh: 邈蒞官簡惠，達于從政，論議精密，當時多諮稟之，觸類辯釋，問則有對。

translations.literal: Miao’s holding of office was simple and benevolent; he was adept at governance; his discussions were precise; people of the time often consulted him, and he would sort every category with clarifying explanations, answering whatever was asked.
translations.idiomatic: His administration was lean and kind, his judgment sharp; contemporaries constantly sought his opinion and he answered every query with lucid analysis.

sentences.zh: 舊疑歲辰在卯，此宅之左則彼宅之右，何得俱忌於東。

translations.literal: An old doubt held that when the year-branch is mao, this house’s left is that house’s right—how can both be taboo on the east?
translations.idiomatic: A standing puzzle: in a mao year the "left" of one dwelling is another’s "right"—how can both ban the east?

sentences.zh: 邈以為太歲之屬，自是遊神，譬如日出之時，向東皆逆，非為藏體地中也。

translations.literal: Miao held that the domains of the Grand Year spirit are themselves roaming gods; it is like the moment of sunrise, when facing east is everywhere contrary—it does not mean the body is buried in the ground.
translations.idiomatic: Xu Miao argued the Grand Year deity moves like the sun at dawn—east is universally inauspicious for that hour, not a fixed spot underground.

sentences.zh: 所注《穀梁傳》，見重于時。

translations.literal: His commentary on the Guliang tradition was esteemed in the age.
translations.idiomatic: His Guliang commentary won wide respect.

sentences.zh: 邈長子豁，有父風，以孝聞，為太常博士、秘書郎。

translations.literal: Miao’s eldest son Huo had his father’s manner, was famed for filial piety, and served as erudite of the chamberlain of ceremonies and palace secretary.
translations.idiomatic: Eldest son Huo inherited his father’s character, was noted for filial piety, and held posts as ritual erudite and palace secretary.

sentences.zh: 豁弟浩，散騎侍郎。

translations.literal: Huo’s younger brother Hao was gentleman cavalier attendant.
translations.idiomatic: Younger brother Hao was gentleman cavalier attendant.

sentences.zh: 鎮南將軍何無忌請為功曹，出補西陽太守，與無忌俱為盧循所害。

translations.literal: The general who guards the south, He Wuji, invited him as merit assessor; he went out to fill governor of Xiyang, and together with Wuji was killed by Lu Xun.
translations.idiomatic: General He Wuji made him merit assessor, then governor of Xiyang; both fell to Lu Xun’s forces.

sentences.zh: 邈弟廣，別有傳。

translations.literal: Miao’s younger brother Guang has a separate biography.
translations.idiomatic: Brother Guang appears in another chapter.

sentences.zh: 孔衍

translations.literal: Kong Yan
translations.idiomatic: Kong Yan

sentences.zh: 孔衍，字舒元，魯國人，孔子二十二世孫也。

translations.literal: Kong Yan, styled Shuyuan, was a man of the state of Lu, the twenty-second-generation descendant of Confucius.
translations.idiomatic: Kong Yan, courtesy Shuyuan, of Lu, was twenty-two generations removed from Confucius.

sentences.zh: 祖文，魏大鴻臚。

translations.literal: His grandfather Wen was grand herald for Wei.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Wen had been Wei’s grand herald.

sentences.zh: 父毓，征南軍司。

translations.literal: His father Yu was marshal to the general who campaigns south.
translations.idiomatic: His father Kong Yu had been marshal on the staff of the southern campaign commander.

sentences.zh: 衍少好學，年十二，能通《詩》《書》。

translations.literal: Yan from youth loved learning; at twelve he could penetrate the Poetry and the Documents.
translations.idiomatic: Kong Yan loved books; by twelve he had mastered the Poetry and the Documents.

sentences.zh: 弱冠，公府辟，本州舉異行直言，皆不就。

translations.literal: At the capping age the ducal offices summoned him, and his province nominated him for unusual conduct and outspoken integrity, but in each case he did not go.
translations.idiomatic: He came of age to ministerial summons and a provincial nomination for exceptional candor, yet refused every post.

sentences.zh: 避地江東，元帝引為安東參軍，專掌記室。

translations.literal: Fleeing trouble he went east of the Yangzi; Emperor Yuan brought him in as staff adviser to the general who pacifies the east, exclusively managing the secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: Sheltering in the southeast, Emperor Yuan named him adviser on Sima Rui’s staff, in charge of the records office.

sentences.zh: 書令殷積，而衍每以稱職見知。

translations.literal: Written orders piled up, yet Yan each time was recognized as competent in office.
translations.idiomatic: Memoranda stacked high, but Kong Yan always proved equal to the workload.

sentences.zh: 中興初，與庚亮俱補中書郎。

translations.literal: At the beginning of the restoration he and Yu Liang were both appointed gentlemen of the secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Eastern Jin revival he and Yu Liang jointly became secretariat gentlemen.

sentences.zh: 明帝之在東宮，領太子中庶子。

translations.literal: When Emperor Ming was in the Eastern Palace, Yan served as junior tutor to the heir apparent.
translations.idiomatic: While still crown prince, Emperor Ming kept him as junior tutor to the heir.

sentences.zh: 于時庶事草創，衍經學深博，又練識舊典，朝儀軌制多取正焉。

translations.literal: At that time myriad tasks were first being founded; Yan’s classical learning was deep and broad, and he was practiced in old precedents, so court ceremonies and regulations mostly took correction from him.
translations.idiomatic: With the new court still improvising, Kong Yan’s command of precedent shaped most ritual and bureaucracy.

sentences.zh: 由是元明二帝並親愛之。

translations.literal: Thereby both Emperors Yuan and Ming personally loved him.
translations.idiomatic: Both Yuan and Ming held him in affectionate esteem.

sentences.zh: 王敦專權，衍私于太子曰：「殿下宜博延朝彥，搜揚才俊，詢謀時政，以廣聖聰。

translations.literal: Wang Dun monopolized power; Yan privately said to the heir apparent: "Your Highness ought broadly to extend court elites, search out and raise talented men, consult on the policies of the times, and thereby broaden sagely listening.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun’s dictatorship moved Kong Yan to urge the crown prince: "Summon worthy ministers, seek out talent, debate policy—widen the throne’s perspective.

sentences.zh: 」敦聞而惡之，乃啟出衍為廣陵郡。

translations.literal: When Dun heard of it he hated Yan, and thereupon had him sent out as governor of Guangling commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun, hearing of it, banished him to Guangling.

sentences.zh: 時人為之寒心，而衍不形於色。

translations.literal: People of the time were chilled for him, yet Yan did not show it in his expression.
translations.idiomatic: Onlookers trembled for him; Kong Yan’s face never changed.

sentences.zh: 雖郡鄰接西賊，猶教誘後進，不以戎務廢業。

translations.literal: Although the commandery bordered the western rebels, he still taught and encouraged later students, not letting military affairs waste his vocation.
translations.idiomatic: Even on a frontier with enemy territory he kept teaching and never let war cancel scholarship.

sentences.zh: 石勒嘗騎至山陽，敕其党以衍儒雅之士，不得妄入郡境。

translations.literal: Shi Le once rode as far as Shanyang and ordered his followers that Yan was a Ru scholar of refinement and must not rashly enter the commandery’s territory.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Le reached Shanyang but warned his men that Kong Yan was a gentleman scholar whose lands they must not violate.

sentences.zh: 視職期月，乙卒於官，年五十三。

translations.literal: After serving in office one full month, he died in post, aged fifty-three.
translations.idiomatic: He died in office within a month of taking up the post, at fifty-three.

sentences.zh: 衍雖不以文才著稱，而博覽過於賀循，凡所撰述，百餘萬言。

translations.literal: Although Yan was not famed for literary talent, his broad reading exceeded that of He Xun; in all, what he composed runs to more than a million characters.
translations.idiomatic: He was no stylistic star, yet he out-read He Xun and left over a million graphs of writing.

sentences.zh: 子啟，盧陵太守。

translations.literal: His son Qi was governor of Luling.
translations.idiomatic: His son Kong Qi governed Luling.

sentences.zh: 宗人夷吾，有美名，博學不及衍，涉世聲譽過之。

translations.literal: A clansman Yiwu had a fair reputation; in broad learning he did not match Yan, but in worldly repute he surpassed him.
translations.idiomatic: Kinsman Kong Yiwu enjoyed a polished name—less learned than Kong Yan, better known in society.

sentences.zh: 元帝以為主簿，轉參軍，稍遷侍中，徙太子左衛率，卒，追贈太僕。

translations.literal: Emperor Yuan made him chief clerk, transferred him to staff adviser, gradually promoted him to palace attendant, moved him to commander of the heir’s left guard, and when he died posthumously awarded minister of works.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan advanced him from chief clerk to attendant and left guard commander; at death he received the posthumous title of minister of works.

sentences.zh: 范宣

translations.literal: Fan Xuan
translations.idiomatic: Fan Xuan

sentences.zh: 范宣，字宣子，陳留人也。

translations.literal: Fan Xuan, styled Xuanzi, was a man of Chenliu.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Xuan, courtesy Xuanzi, came from Chenliu.

sentences.zh: 年十歲，能誦《詩》《書》。

translations.literal: At age ten he could recite the Poetry and the Documents.
translations.idiomatic: At ten he knew the Poetry and Documents by heart.

sentences.zh: 嘗以刀傷手，捧手改容。

translations.literal: Once he cut his hand with a knife; he cupped the hand and changed expression.
translations.idiomatic: He once gashed his hand with a knife and studied the wound gravely.

sentences.zh: 人問痛邪，答曰：「不足為痛，但受全之體而致毀傷，不可處耳。

translations.literal: Someone asked whether it hurt; he replied, "It is not worth calling pain, but this body was received whole from my parents; to bring injury upon it is something I cannot abide."
translations.idiomatic: Asked if it hurt, he said the pain was nothing, but mutilating the body his parents gave him was unbearable.

sentences.zh: 」家人以其年幼而異焉。

translations.literal: His family thought him extraordinary for one so young.
translations.idiomatic: His household marveled at such words from a child.

sentences.zh: 少尚隱遁，加以好學，手不釋卷，以夜繼日，遂博綜眾書，尤善《三禮》。

translations.literal: In youth he esteemed reclusion; added to love of learning, his hand never released a scroll, continuing day into night, whereupon he broadly synthesized the many books and was especially adept in the Three Rites.
translations.idiomatic: Youthful love of seclusion and books kept him reading night and day until he commanded every corpus, above all the three ritual classics.

sentences.zh: 家至貧儉，躬耕供養。

translations.literal: His home reached the utmost in poverty and frugality; he personally plowed to supply his parents.
translations.idiomatic: Destitute, he farmed to feed his elders.

sentences.zh: 親沒，負土成墳，廬於墓側。

translations.literal: When his parents died he carried earth to complete the mounds and built a hut beside the graves.
translations.idiomatic: He piled the burial mounds with his own hands and mourned in a hut at their side.

sentences.zh: 太尉郗鑒命為主簿，詔徵太學博士、散騎郎，並不就。

translations.literal: Grand commandant Xi Jian ordered him chief clerk; edicts summoned him as erudite of the imperial academy and gentleman cavalier attendant, but he accepted none of these.
translations.idiomatic: Xi Jian wanted him as chief clerk; court summons to the academy and cavalier posts went unanswered.

sentences.zh: 家于豫章，太守殷羨見宣茅茨不完，欲為改宅，宣固辭之。

translations.literal: He made his home in Yuzhang; Governor Yin Xian saw that Xuan’s thatch roof was incomplete and wished to build him a new house, but Xuan firmly declined.
translations.idiomatic: Living in Yuzhang under Yin Xian, he refused a new house when the governor saw his leaking roof.

sentences.zh: 庾爰之以宣素貧，加年荒疾疫，厚餉給之，宣又不受。

translations.literal: Yu Yuanshi, because Xuan was always poor and added to that there were years of famine and epidemic, richly supplied him, but again Xuan would not accept.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Yuanshi sent generous relief during famine and plague; Fan Xuan still refused.

sentences.zh: 爰之問宣曰：「君博學通綜，何以太儒？

translations.literal: Yuanshi asked Xuan, "You are broadly learned and comprehensive—why are you so extremely Ru?"
translations.idiomatic: Yu Yuanshi asked why, for so learned a man, he clung so stubbornly to old-style Confucianism.

sentences.zh: 」宣曰：「漢興，貴經術，至於石渠之論，實以儒為弊。

translations.literal: Xuan said, "When Han rose it honored classical arts; down to the Shiqu discussions, in truth they took Ru learning as a bane.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Xuan answered: Han’s elevation of the classics culminated in the Shiqu conference—where Ru learning already showed its excesses.

sentences.zh: 正始以來，世尚老莊。

translations.literal: From the Zhengshi era onward, the age esteemed Laozi and Zhuangzi.
translations.idiomatic: After Zhengshi, fashion chased Laozi and Zhuangzi.

sentences.zh: 逮晉之初，競以裸裎為高。

translations.literal: Down to the beginning of Jin, they vied to take nakedness as lofty.
translations.idiomatic: Early Jin society mistook shamelessness for sophistication.

sentences.zh: 僕誠太儒，然'丘不與易'。

translations.literal: I am indeed excessively Ru, yet [Confucius said] 'Qiu would not change it for anything.'"
translations.idiomatic: Call me old-fashioned; as Confucius said, this is not a trend I would join."

sentences.zh: 」宣言談未嘗及《老》《莊》。

translations.literal: Xuan’s conversation never touched on Laozi or Zhuangzi.
translations.idiomatic: He never brought up Daoist texts in discussion.

sentences.zh: 客有問人生與憂俱生，不知此語何出。

translations.literal: A guest asked that human life is born together with care, and did not know where this saying came from.
translations.idiomatic: A visitor quoted Zhuangzi’s line that sorrow attends every life and asked its source.

sentences.zh: 宣云：「出《莊子·至樂篇》。

translations.literal: Xuan said, "It comes from the 'Utmost Joy' chapter of Zhuangzi."
translations.idiomatic: Fan Xuan cited the "Utmost Joy" chapter of Zhuangzi.

sentences.zh: 」客曰：「君言不讀《老》《莊》，何由識此？

translations.literal: The guest said, "You say you do not read Laozi or Zhuangzi—how then do you know this?"
translations.idiomatic: The guest protested: you claim to shun those books, yet you cite them.

sentences.zh: 」宣笑曰：「小時嘗一覽。

translations.literal: Xuan laughed and said, "In youth I once glanced through them."
translations.idiomatic: Fan Xuan smiled: "I skimmed them once as a boy."

sentences.zh: 」時人莫之測也。

translations.literal: People of the time could not fathom him.
translations.idiomatic: Contemporaries never quite pinned him down.

sentences.zh: 宣雖閒居屢空，常以講誦為業，譙國戴逵等皆聞風宗仰，自遠而至，諷誦之聲，有若齊、魯。

translations.literal: Although Xuan lived retired in repeated emptiness, he always took lecturing and recitation as his occupation; Dai Kui of Qiao and others all heard the wind and revered him, coming from afar; the sound of intoning was as if in Qi or Lu.
translations.idiomatic: Despite poverty he taught endlessly; Dai Kui and others crossed counties to study, and the drone of students echoed like old Qi or Lu.

sentences.zh: 太元中，順陽范甯為豫章太守，甯亦儒博通綜，在郡立鄉校，教授恆數百人。

translations.literal: In the Taiyuan years Fan Ning of Shunyang was governor of Yuzhang; Ning likewise was broadly learned in Ru teaching; in the commandery he established village schools, and those under instruction were constantly several hundred.
translations.idiomatic: Under Taiyuan, Fan Ning governed Yuzhang, founded rural schools, and taught hundreds at a time.

sentences.zh: 由是江州人士並好經學，化二范之風也。

translations.literal: Thereby gentlemen of Jiangzhou together loved classical learning—this was transformation by the wind of the two Fans.
translations.idiomatic: Jiangzhou’s passion for the classics was the legacy of both Fans.

sentences.zh: 年五十四卒。

translations.literal: He died at fifty-four.
translations.idiomatic: He died at fifty-four.

sentences.zh: 著《禮》《易論難》皆行於世。

translations.literal: He authored Difficulties on the Rites and on the Changes, each of which circulated in the world.
translations.idiomatic: His Debates on the Rites and on the Changes were widely read.

sentences.zh: 子輯，曆郡守、國子博士、大將軍從事中郎。

translations.literal: His son Ji served in turn as governor of commanderies, erudite of the imperial academy, and staff adviser to the grand general.
translations.idiomatic: Son Fan Ji was commandery governor, academy erudite, and grand-general’s adviser.

sentences.zh: 自免歸，亦以講授為事。

translations.literal: Having resigned on his own initiative, he likewise took lecturing as his task.
translations.idiomatic: After retiring he returned to teaching.

sentences.zh: 義熙中，連徵不至。

translations.literal: In the Yixi years he was summoned repeatedly but did not come.
translations.idiomatic: Yixi-era summons never brought him back to office.

sentences.zh: 韋謏

translations.literal: Wei Sou
translations.idiomatic: Wei Sou

sentences.zh: 韋謏，字憲道，京兆人也。

translations.literal: Wei Sou, styled Xiandao, was a man of Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Sou, courtesy Xiandao, hailed from Jingzhao.

sentences.zh: 雅好儒學，善著述，于群言秘要之義，無不綜覽。

translations.literal: He refined a love of Ru learning and was skilled in composition; as to the essential meanings of the various writers and secret texts, there was none he did not survey.
translations.idiomatic: He cultivated classical scholarship and writing, mastering every major text and esoteric tradition.

sentences.zh: 仕于劉曜，為黃門郎。

translations.literal: He served under Liu Yao as gentleman at the yellow gate.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Yao employed him as a yellow-gate gentleman.

sentences.zh: 後又入石季龍，署為散騎常侍，曆守七郡，咸以清化著名。

translations.literal: Afterward he entered the service of Shi Jilong, who appointed him cavalier attendant-in-ordinary; he successively governed seven commanderies, in each case famed for pure transformation.
translations.idiomatic: Under Shi Hu he became cavalier attendant and governed seven commanderies, each noted for honest rule.

sentences.zh: 又徵為廷尉，識者擬之于、張。

translations.literal: He was again summoned as commandant of trials; knowledgeable men compared him to Yu Dingguo and Zhang Chang.
translations.idiomatic: Recalled as chief justice, experts likened him to the Han paragons Yu and Zhang.

sentences.zh: 前後四登九列，六在尚書，二為侍中，再為太子太傅，封京兆公。

translations.literal: Before and after he ascended the nine columns four times, was six times in the masters of writing, twice palace attendant, twice grand tutor to the heir apparent, and was enfeoffed duke of Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to the top ministries four times, served six terms in the masters of writing, twice as palace attendant, twice as heir’s grand tutor, and held a Jingzhao ducal title.

sentences.zh: 好直諫，陳軍國之宜，多見允納。

translations.literal: He loved straight remonstrance; in stating what suited army and state he was mostly approved and accepted.
translations.idiomatic: His blunt advice on civil and military policy usually won approval.

sentences.zh: 著《伏林》三千餘言，遂演為《典林》二十三篇。

translations.literal: He authored The Hidden Forest in more than three thousand words, then expanded it into The Canon Forest in twenty-three chapters.
translations.idiomatic: He wrote three thousand graphs of The Hidden Forest, later enlarged into twenty-three chapters of The Canon Forest.

sentences.zh: 凡所述作及集記世事數十萬言，皆深博有才義。

translations.literal: In all, his compositions and collected records of current affairs ran to several hundred thousand words, all deep, broad, and rich in talent and meaning.
translations.idiomatic: His collected works and notes on public life exceed several hundred thousand characters of substance.

sentences.zh: 至冉閔，又署為光祿大夫。

translations.literal: Under Ran Min he was again appointed grand master of splendid happiness.
translations.idiomatic: Ran Min named him grand master of splendid happiness.

sentences.zh: 時閔拜其子胤為大單于，而以降胡一千處之麾下。

translations.literal: At that time Min invested his son Yin as grand chanyu and placed a thousand surrendered Hu under his command.
translations.idiomatic: Ran Min then made his son Yin grand chanyu and camped a thousand surrendered Hu troops under him.

sentences.zh: 謏諫曰：「今降胡數千，接之如舊，誠是招誘之恩。

translations.literal: Sou remonstrated: "Now several thousand surrendered Hu are treated as of old—this is indeed the kindness that attracts defectors.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Sou warned: treating thousands of surrendered tribesmen like old allies shows mercy,

sentences.zh: 然胡羯本為仇敵，今之款附，苟全性命耳。

translations.literal: Yet the Hu and Jie were originally mortal enemies; today’s sincere attachment is only a matter of preserving their lives for the moment.
translations.idiomatic: but Hu and Jie were blood foes; their submission is mere survival,

sentences.zh: 或有刺客，變起須臾，敗而悔之，何所及也！

translations.literal: Should assassins arise, a revolt could come in an instant—defeated, you would regret it, but what remedy would there be!
translations.idiomatic: and assassins could strike before you know it—then regret would be useless!

sentences.zh: 古人有言，一夫不可狃，而況千乎！

translations.literal: The ancients had a saying: one man must not be treated with contempt—how much more a thousand!
translations.idiomatic: The proverb says never despise even one man—let alone a thousand!

sentences.zh: 願誅屏降胡，去單于之號，深思聖五苞桑之誡也。

translations.literal: I beg to execute or banish the surrendered Hu, remove the title of chanyu, and ponder deeply the sage’s warning about binding the state to mulberry roots [from the Changes]."
translations.idiomatic: Kill or expel them, strip the chanyu title, and heed the Classic of Changes’ warning about securing the realm."

sentences.zh: 」閔志在綏撫，銳於澄定，聞其言，大怒，遂誅之，並殺其子伯陽。

translations.literal: Min’s aim was to pacify and comfort; he was keen on settling things; hearing these words, he was greatly angered, thereupon executed Sou and also killed his son Boyang.
translations.idiomatic: Ran Min wanted reconciliation; enraged by the advice, he executed Wei Sou and his son Boyang.

sentences.zh: 謏性不嚴重，好徇己之功，論者亦以是少之。

translations.literal: Sou’s nature was not stern and weighty; he liked to pursue his own achievements, and critics on this account slighted him.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Sou was light-minded and vain of his feats—commentators faulted him for it.

sentences.zh: 嘗謂伯陽曰：「我高我曾重光累徽，我祖我考父父子子，汝為我對，正值惡抵。

translations.literal: He once said to Boyang, "My high ancestors piled glory upon glory; my grandfathers and fathers in succession—now you make a matching phrase, and it comes out 'evil buttress.'"
translations.idiomatic: He quizzed his son on a couplet bragging of ancestors; Boyang’s answer sounded like "wicked prop."

sentences.zh: 」伯陽曰：「伯陽之不肖，誠如尊教，尊亦正值軟抵耳。

translations.literal: Boyang said, "Boyang’s lack of talent is indeed as you instruct; you likewise come out only as 'soft buttress.'"
translations.idiomatic: The boy shot back that his father’s line was no better—just "limp support."

sentences.zh: 」謏慚無言。

translations.literal: Sou was ashamed and had nothing to say.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Sou had no reply.

sentences.zh: 時人傳之，以為嗤笑。

translations.literal: People of the time passed the story around as a joke.
translations.idiomatic: The courtiers turned it into a standing joke.

sentences.zh: 范弘之

translations.literal: Fan Hongzhi
translations.idiomatic: Fan Hongzhi

sentences.zh: 范弘之，字長文，安北將軍汪之孫也。

translations.literal: Fan Hongzhi, styled Zhangwen, was the grandson of the general who pacifies the north, Fan Wang.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Hongzhi, courtesy Zhangwen, was grandson of Fan Wang, general who pacifies the north.

sentences.zh: 襲爵武興侯。

translations.literal: He inherited the marquisate of Wuxing.
translations.idiomatic: He inherited the Wuxing marquisate.

sentences.zh: 雅正好學，以儒術該明，為太學博士。

translations.literal: Refined, upright, and fond of learning, with Ru arts comprehensive and clear, he became erudite of the imperial academy.
translations.idiomatic: A polished scholar, he rose to academy erudite.

sentences.zh: 時衛將軍謝石薨，請諡，下禮官議。

translations.literal: When the general who guards the guards Xie Shi died, a posthumous name was requested; it was sent down to the ritual officials for deliberation.
translations.idiomatic: Xie Shi’s death triggered a posthumous title debate among ritual officers.

sentences.zh: 弘之議曰：

translations.literal: Hongzhi’s opinion stated:
translations.idiomatic: Fan Hongzhi argued:

sentences.zh: 石階藉門廕，屢登崇顯，總司百揆，翼贊三台，閑練庶事，勤勞匪懈，內外僉議，皆曰與能。

translations.literal: Shi, relying on gate and shade, repeatedly ascended to lofty display; he overall managed the hundred responsibilities, assisted and adorned the three terraces, was practiced in the myriad tasks, and toiled without slackening; inside and outside the unanimous judgment was that he matched the able.
translations.idiomatic: Xie Shi rode family privilege to high office, ran the bureaucracy, aided the three councils, knew every portfolio, and worked tirelessly—many called him competent.

sentences.zh: 當淮肥之捷，勳拯危墜，雖皇威遐震，狡寇天亡，因時立功，石亦與焉。

translations.literal: At the victory on the Huai and Fei, his merit rescued the perilous and falling; although imperial majesty shook afar and the crafty foe perished as Heaven decreed, seizing the moment to achieve merit, Shi also had a share.
translations.idiomatic: At Feishui he helped save the dynasty; heaven and the emperor’s prestige broke the enemy, yet he earned a share of the credit.

sentences.zh: 又開建學校，以延胄子，雖盛化未洽，亦愛禮存羊。

translations.literal: Further he opened and built schools to extend the scions of nobles; although the great transformation was not yet pervasive, it was still a case of loving ritual and keeping the sheep [symbol].
translations.idiomatic: He founded schools for noble heirs—imperfect reform, but like Confucius keeping the sheep to preserve ritual.

sentences.zh: 然古之賢輔，大則以道事君，侃侃終日；

translations.literal: Yet the ancient worthy assistants, at the greatest, served the ruler with the Way, speaking forthrightly all day long;
translations.idiomatic: True ministers of old served with the Way and spoke boldly without cease;

sentences.zh: 次則厲身奉國，夙夜無怠；

translations.literal: at the next rank they disciplined themselves to serve the state, toiling morning and night without slack;
translations.idiomatic: the next rank gave body and soul to the state night and day;

sentences.zh: 下則愛人惜力，以濟時務。

translations.literal: at the lowest they loved the people and husbanded strength to aid the tasks of the times.
translations.idiomatic: the humblest loved the people and saved their strength for the age’s needs.

sentences.zh: 此數者，然後可以免惟塵之議，塞素餐之責矣。

translations.literal: Only after these several could one escape blame for trailing dust and block censure for eating an empty salary.
translations.idiomatic: Only thus could they avoid the charge of trailing dust in the ruler’s train or eating free bread.

sentences.zh: 今石位居朝端，任則論道，唱言無忠國之謀，守職則容身而已，不可謂事君；

translations.literal: Now Shi occupies the head of court; his charge is to discourse on the Way; when he opens his mouth there are no loyal plans for the state, and in guarding office he only accommodates himself—this cannot be called serving the ruler.
translations.idiomatic: Xie Shi reached the summit yet offered no loyal counsel—only self-preservation—that is not serving a lord.

sentences.zh: 貨黷京邑，聚斂無厭，不可謂厲身；

translations.literal: He trafficked bribes in the capital, amassing without satiety—this cannot be called disciplining himself.
translations.idiomatic: He sold offices in the capital and hoarded wealth—that is not self-discipline.

sentences.zh: 坐擁大眾，侵食百姓，《大東》流於遠近，怨毒結於眾心，不可謂愛人；

translations.literal: He sat possessing great hosts, encroaching on and devouring the hundred surnames; the ode Great East flowed far and near, resentment and poison knotted in the hearts of the multitude—this cannot be called loving the people.
translations.idiomatic: He squeezed the commoners until the Poetry’s Great East seemed written for him—that is not loving the people.

sentences.zh: 工徒勞於土木，思慮殫於機巧，紈綺盡於婢妾，財用縻於絲桐，不可謂惜力。

translations.literal: Craftsmen toiled at earth and wood; thought exhausted itself in ingenious devices; fine silks were exhausted on slave girls; wealth was squandered on lutes—this cannot be called husbanding strength.
translations.idiomatic: Labor wasted on palaces, wit on toys, silk on concubines, treasure on music—that is not husbanding strength.

sentences.zh: 此人臣之大害，有國之所去也。

translations.literal: These are the great harms of ministers and what a state casts off.
translations.idiomatic: Such conduct is the worst in a minister and what any state should reject.

sentences.zh: 先王所以正風俗，理人倫者，莫尚乎節儉，故夷吾受謗乎三歸，平仲流美於約己。

translations.literal: What the former kings used to rectify customs and order human relations none valued more than frugality; therefore Guan Zhong suffered slander for his three returning treasures, while Yan Ying left beauty in restraining himself.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient kings reformed manners through thrift—Guan Zhong was mocked for excess, Yan Ying praised for restraint.

sentences.zh: 自頃風軌陵遲，奢僭無度，廉恥不興，利競交馳，不可不深防原本，以絕其流。

translations.literal: Recently standards have declined, extravagance and usurpation know no limit, integrity and shame do not rise, profit races in every quarter—one cannot fail deeply to guard the root source in order to cut off this current.
translations.idiomatic: Today fashion runs to waste and shameless greed; we must strike at the root.

sentences.zh: 漢文襲弋綈之服，諸侯猶侈；

translations.literal: Emperor Wen of Han wore black silk robes, yet the feudal lords were still extravagant;
translations.idiomatic: Han Wendi’s plain dress failed to stop noble excess;

sentences.zh: 武帝焚雉頭之裘，靡麗不息。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu burned the pheasant-feather cloak, yet wasteful splendor did not cease.
translations.idiomatic: Han Wudi’s bonfire of luxuries never ended ostentation.

sentences.zh: 良由儉德雖彰，而威禁不肅；

translations.literal: Truly it is because although the virtue of frugality was displayed, awesome prohibition was not strict;
translations.idiomatic: Personal example alone lacks teeth;

sentences.zh: 道自我建，而刑不及物。

translations.literal: the Way was established from oneself, yet punishments did not reach things.
translations.idiomatic: moral suasion without enforcement changes nothing.

sentences.zh: 若存罰其違，亡貶其惡，則四維必張，禮義行矣。

translations.literal: If while alive we punish the violators and after death we degrade the wicked, then the four bonds will surely be stretched tight and ritual and righteousness will operate.
translations.idiomatic: Punish the living, shame the dead, and the four social ties tighten—ritual revives.

sentences.zh: 案諡法，因事有功曰「襄」，貪以敗官曰「墨」，宜諡曰襄墨公。

translations.literal: According to the posthumous canon, merit through affairs is called 'Xiang,' covetousness that ruins office is called 'Mo'; the appropriate posthumous name should be Duke Xiang-Mo.
translations.idiomatic: By the naming code, "Xiang" marks battlefield success, "Mo" marks corrupt office—call him Duke Xiang-Mo.

sentences.zh: 又論殷浩宜加贈諡，不得因桓溫之黜以為國典，仍多敘溫移鼎之跡。

translations.literal: He further argued that Yin Hao ought to receive posthumous honors and that Huan Wen’s demotion of him must not be taken as national precedent, going on at length to narrate Huan Wen’s traces of shifting the tripods.
translations.idiomatic: He also demanded posthumous honors for Yin Hao, insisting Huan Wen’s disgrace of him must not set precedent, and recounted Huan Wen’s usurpation-minded career at length.

sentences.zh: 時謝族方顯，桓宗猶盛，尚書僕射王珣，溫故吏也，素為溫所寵，三怨交集，乃出弘之為余杭令。

translations.literal: At that time the Xie clan was just prominent, the Huan lineage still strong, and Vice Director of the Masters of Writing Wang Xun, a former subordinate of Wen, had long been favored by Wen; the three resentments converged, and thereupon Hongzhi was sent out as magistrate of Yuhang.
translations.idiomatic: The Xies were ascendant, the Huans still powerful, and Wang Xun—Huan Wen’s old protégé—resented Fan Hongzhi’s memorial alongside two other grudges, so the court banished him to Yuhang county.

sentences.zh: 將行，與會稽王道子箋曰：

translations.literal: About to depart, he wrote Prince Kuaiji, Sima Daozi, a note saying:
translations.idiomatic: Before leaving he sent Prince Kuaiji this letter:

sentences.zh: 下官輕微寒士，謬得廁在俎豆，實懼辱累清流，惟塵聖世。

translations.literal: Your lowly official, a slight man of cold pedigree, wrongly gained a place among the sacrificial vessels; I truly fear bringing shame upon the clear current and trailing dust upon a sagely age.
translations.idiomatic: I am a nobody who stumbled into court ritual; I dread smearing the pure stream and clouding an enlightened reign.

sentences.zh: 竊以人君居廟堂之上、智周四海之外者，非徒聰明內照，亦賴群言之助也。

translations.literal: I privately consider that a ruler who sits above the temple hall yet whose wisdom circles beyond the four seas does not rely solely on inner brilliance but also depends on the aid of collective counsel.
translations.idiomatic: A sovereign needs more than native wit—he needs the chorus of honest advisers.

sentences.zh: 是以舜之佐堯，以啟辟為首；

translations.literal: Therefore when Shun assisted Yao, he placed foremost opening and correcting the ruler’s mind;
translations.idiomatic: Shun served Yao by speaking truth to power;

sentences.zh: 咎繇謨禹，以侃侃為先，故下無隱情之責，上收神明之功。

translations.literal: when Gao Yao counseled Yu, he put bold forthrightness first, so that below there was no hidden feeling left unspoken and above the work of spiritual intelligence was gathered.
translations.idiomatic: Gao Yao aided Yu with blunt counsel, leaving no secrets below and winning clarity above.

sentences.zh: 敢緣斯義，志在輸盡。

translations.literal: Daring to follow this principle, my aim is to pour out everything.
translations.idiomatic: I mean to speak plainly on that model.

sentences.zh: 常以謝石黷累，應被清澄，殷浩忠貞，宜蒙褒顯，是以不量輕弱，先眾言之。

translations.literal: I have always held that Xie Shi, stained by corruption, ought to be purged, and Yin Hao, loyal and steadfast, ought to receive honor; therefore, not measuring my weakness, I spoke ahead of the crowd.
translations.idiomatic: I said Xie Shi deserved censure and Yin Hao posthumous honor, and spoke first though I am slight.

sentences.zh: 而惡直醜正。

translations.literal: Yet straightness is hated and integrity mocked.
translations.idiomatic: But the powerful despise candor.

sentences.zh: 其徒實繁，雖仰恃聖主欽明之度，俯賴明公愛物之隆，而交至之患，實有無賴。

translations.literal: Their faction is truly numerous; although I look up and rely on the sagely ruler’s enlightened measure, and look down and rely on your lordship’s lofty care for creatures, the affliction of converging attacks truly has no limit.
translations.idiomatic: Their party is huge; I trust the emperor’s wisdom and your fairness, yet coordinated malice knows no bounds.

sentences.zh: 下官與石本無怨忌，生不相識，事無相干，正以國體宜明，不應稍計強弱。

translations.literal: Your lowly official and Shi originally had no resentment or jealousy; we were not acquainted in life, and affairs did not intersect—only because the body politic ought to be transparent did I refuse to calculate strength and weakness.
translations.idiomatic: I had no feud with Xie Shi; I spoke for the state, not for private power.

sentences.zh: 與浩年時邈絕，世不相及，無復藉聞，故老語其遺事耳，於下官之身有何痛癢，而當為之犯時幹主邪！

translations.literal: With Hao my ages are utterly remote, our generations do not meet, I have no borrowed hearsay—only old men tell his leftover stories—what itch or pain does this mean for my person, that I should offend the times and resist the ruler!
translations.idiomatic: Yin Hao lived generations before me; I know him only by legend—why would I risk my neck except for public duty?

sentences.zh: 每觀載籍，志士仁人有發中心任直道而行者，有懷知陽愚負情曲從者，所用雖異，而並傳後世。

translations.literal: Whenever I read the records, resolute gentlemen and humane men include those who spoke from the center and walked the straight way, and those who hid knowledge, feigned foolishness, and bent emotion in compliant following; although what they used differed, both are transmitted to later ages.
translations.idiomatic: History honors both blunt martyrs and tactful survivors.

sentences.zh: 故比干處三仁之中，箕子為名賢之首。

translations.literal: Therefore Bi Gan stands among the three humane men, and Jizi heads the list of famed worthies.
translations.idiomatic: Hence Bi Gan ranks among the three paragons, Jizi among the greatest sages.

sentences.zh: 後人用舍，參差不同，各信所見，率應而至，或榮名顯赫，或禍敗系踵，此皆不量時趣，以身嘗禍，雖有硜硜之稱，而非大雅之致，此亦下官所不為也。

translations.literal: Later people’s employment or rejection differed unevenly; each trusted his own view and responded as led—some gained glorious fame, some disaster followed on their heels; all these failed to measure the temper of the times and tasted calamity with their bodies; although they had the reputation of stubbornness, they did not reach the demeanor of great elegance—this likewise is what your lowly official will not do.
translations.idiomatic: Later readers pick sides; some win fame, some ruin—those who misread their moment earn a stubborn name but not true greatness; that is not my path.

sentences.zh: 世人乃雲下官正直，能犯艱難，斯談實過。

translations.literal: Yet the world says your lowly official is upright and can brave hardship—such talk truly overstates it.
translations.idiomatic: They call me fearless; that flatters me.

sentences.zh: 下官知主上聖明，明公虛己，思求格言，必不使盡忠之臣屈於邪枉之門也。

translations.literal: Your lowly official knows the ruler is sagely enlightened, and your lordship empties yourself, seeking fine words—you surely will not let a minister who exhausted loyalty be bent under a gate of wicked perversity.
translations.idiomatic: I trust the throne and you seek honest words—you will not let loyalty be crushed by crooks.

sentences.zh: 是以敢獻愚誠，布之執事，豈與昔人擬其輕重邪！

translations.literal: Therefore I dare offer foolish sincerity and spread it before the steward—how could I compare weight with men of old!
translations.idiomatic: So I lay out my heart—not matching antiquity’s heroes, only doing my duty.

sentences.zh: 亦以臣之事君，惟思盡忠而已，不應復計利鈍，事不允心則讜言悟主，義感于情則陳辭靡悔。

translations.literal: Likewise, in the matter of a subject serving a ruler, I only think to exhaust loyalty; one ought not again calculate sharp or dull; when affairs do not accord with the mind, then blunt words awaken the ruler; when righteousness stirs feeling, then stated remonstrance knows no regret.
translations.idiomatic: A minister owes full loyalty regardless of cost; if policy offends conscience, speak—even at peril.

sentences.zh: 若懷情藏意，蘊而不言，此乃古人所以得罪于明君，明君所以致法於群下者也。

translations.literal: If one harbors feeling and hides intent, storing it and not speaking—this is how the ancients offended enlightened rulers, and enlightened rulers applied law to the multitude below.
translations.idiomatic: Silence is how subjects betrayed sage kings and kings punished silence.

sentences.zh: 桓溫事蹟，布在天朝，逆順之情，暴之四海。

translations.literal: Huan Wen’s deeds are spread through the celestial court; the facts of rebellion and submission are exposed to the four seas.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen’s record is public; rebel or loyal, all know.

sentences.zh: 在三者臣子，情豈或異！

translations.literal: Among subjects and sons bound by the three [great bonds], how could feeling differ!
translations.idiomatic: Every man still bound by those duties feels the same!

sentences.zh: 凡厥黔首，誰獨無心！

translations.literal: Of all the black-haired people, who alone lacks a heart!
translations.idiomatic: Which commoner lacks judgment?

sentences.zh: 舉朝嘿嘿，未有唱言者，是以頓筆按氣，不敢多雲。

translations.literal: The whole court is silent; none has spoken up—therefore I set down the brush and suppress my breath, not daring to say much.
translations.idiomatic: Yet the court stays mute, so I hesitate to add more.

sentences.zh: 桓溫于亡祖，雖其意難測，求之於事，止免黜耳，非有至怨也。

translations.literal: Huan Wen toward my deceased grandfather—although his intention is hard to fathom, seeking it in the facts, it stopped at dismissal from office; there was no extreme hatred.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen’s dealings with my grandfather went no further than demotion—no blood feud.

sentences.zh: 亡父昔為溫吏，推之情禮，義兼他人。

translations.literal: My deceased father once served as Wen’s clerk; pushing feeling and ritual, the righteousness extends beyond others.
translations.idiomatic: My father was his clerk, so obligation runs deeper than for most.

sentences.zh: 所以每懷憤發，痛若身首者，明公有以尋之。

translations.literal: The reason I always harbor indignant fervor, pained as if in body and head, your lordship has the means to trace.
translations.idiomatic: You can see why I burn with personal as well as public grief.

sentences.zh: 王珣以下官議殷浩諡，不宜暴揚桓溫之惡。

translations.literal: Wang Xun, because your lowly official argued Yin Hao’s posthumous name, held that one ought not publicly broadcast Huan Wen’s evils.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xun resented my Yin Hao piece for exposing Huan Wen.

sentences.zh: 珣感其提拔之恩，懷其入幕之遇，托以廢黜昏暗，建立聖明，自謂此事足以明其忠貞之節。

translations.literal: Xun, feeling his obligation for being raised in favor, cherishing his encounter of entering the curtain [as staff], pleads that he deposed a dim ruler and established a sagely bright one, himself thinking this affair sufficient to display his loyal and chaste integrity.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xun, grateful for patronage, claims deposing the emperor proved loyalty.

sentences.zh: 明公試復以一事觀之。

translations.literal: Let your lordship try again to observe it through one matter.
translations.idiomatic: Judge the case by one test.

sentences.zh: 昔周公居攝，道致升平，禮樂刑政皆自己出。

translations.literal: Long ago the Duke of Zhou held the regency; the Way brought rising peace; ritual, music, punishments, and government all issued from himself.
translations.idiomatic: The Duke of Zhou ruled as regent and perfected government.

sentences.zh: 以德言之，周公大聖，以年言之，成王幼弱，猶復遽避君位，復子明辭。

translations.literal: Judging by virtue, the Duke of Zhou was a great sage; judging by age, King Cheng was young and weak; still he hastened to yield the ruler’s position and returned the bright mandate to his nephew.
translations.idiomatic: Though Cheng was a child, the duke returned power.

sentences.zh: 漢之霍光，大勳赫然，孝宣年未二十，亦反萬機。

translations.literal: Huo Guang of Han, his great merit blazing, faced Emperor Xuan not yet twenty, who likewise took back the myriad threads.
translations.idiomatic: Huo Guang’s greatness did not stop young Xuandi from resuming rule.

sentences.zh: 故能君臣俱隆，道邁千歲。

translations.literal: Therefore ruler and minister could both flourish, and the Way surpassed a thousand years.
translations.idiomatic: Thus both sides prospered for the ages.

sentences.zh: 若溫忠為社稷，誠存本朝，便當仰遵二公，式是令矩，何不奉還萬機，退守籓屏？

translations.literal: If Wen had been loyal to the altars of soil and grain and sincerely preserved this court, he ought reverently to have followed those two dukes and taken their statutes as model—why not hand back the myriad threads and retire to guard a princely screen?
translations.idiomatic: Had Huan Wen truly served the state, he would have imitated Zhou and Huo and returned the regency.

sentences.zh: 方提勒公王，匡總朝廷，豈為先帝幼弱，未可親政邪？

translations.literal: Instead he seized the dukes and princes, corrected and oversaw the court—was it because the late emperor was young and weak and could not personally govern?
translations.idiomatic: Instead he dominated lords and court—because the boy emperor could not rule?

sentences.zh: 將德桓溫，不能聽政邪？

translations.literal: Or was it that you deferred to Huan Wen and could not administer government?
translations.idiomatic: Or because you deferred to Huan Wen and could not govern yourself?

sentences.zh: 又逼脅袁宏，使作九錫，備物光赫，其文具存，朝廷畏怖，莫不景從，惟謝安、王坦之以死守之，故得稽留耳。

translations.literal: Further he coerced Yuan Hong into drafting the nine bestowals; the ritual vessels blazed with splendor; the document still exists; the court feared and trembled, none did not follow like a shadow—only Xie An and Wang Tanzhi, by dying resolve, held it off, and therefore it could be delayed.
translations.idiomatic: He forced Yuan Hong to craft the nine-scepter petition; the text survives; the court quailed—only Xie An and Wang Tanzhi blocked him until Heaven struck him down.

sentences.zh: 會上天降怒，奸惡自亡，社稷危而復安，靈命墜而復構。

translations.literal: When Heaven above sent down wrath, the traitors destroyed themselves; the altars of soil and grain were perilous yet became secure again; the numinous mandate fell yet was reconstituted.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven removed the traitor; the dynasty rose from the brink.

sentences.zh: 晉自中興以來，號令威權多出強臣，中宗、肅祖斂衽于王敦，先皇受屈於桓氏。

translations.literal: Since Jin’s restoration, commands and awesomely weighty authority have mostly issued from powerful ministers; Emperor Zhongzong and Emperor Suzu drew in their sashes before Wang Dun, and the late emperor suffered insult from the Huan clan.
translations.idiomatic: Eastern Jin long bowed to strongmen—Wang Dun, then Huans.

sentences.zh: 今主上親覽萬機，明公光贊百揆，政出王室，人無異望，復不於今大明國典，作制百代，不審復欲待誰？

translations.literal: Now the ruler personally oversees the myriad threads; your lordship gloriously assists the hundred responsibilities; government issues from the royal house and people harbor no divergent hopes—if not now to clarify the national statutes and establish institutions for a hundred generations, whom do you intend to wait for?
translations.idiomatic: The emperor rules; you assist—if not now to codify justice for posterity, when?

sentences.zh: 先王統物，必明其典誥，貽厥孫謀，故令問休嘉，千歲承風。

translations.literal: The former kings, in ordering things, invariably made clear their canons and instructions, bequeathing plans to their grandsons, so that their fair renown flourished and a thousand years inherited the wind.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient kings left clear precedents for heirs to follow.

sentences.zh: 願明公遠覽殷周，近察漢魏，慮其所以危，求其所以安，如此而已。

translations.literal: I wish your lordship to look far at Yin and Zhou, examine near Han and Wei, ponder why they fell into peril, seek why they found peace—nothing more than this.
translations.idiomatic: Study old dynasties’ falls and rises—that is all I ask.

sentences.zh: 又與王珣書曰：

translations.literal: He also wrote Wang Xun a letter saying:
translations.idiomatic: He also wrote Wang Xun:

sentences.zh: 見足下答仲堪書，深具義發之懷。

translations.literal: Seeing your reply to Zhongkan’s letter, it deeply embodies the mood of righteous declaration.
translations.idiomatic: Your answer to Yin Zhongkan shows noble intent.

sentences.zh: 夫人道所重，莫過君親，君親所系，忠孝而已。

translations.literal: Among human ways none is weightier than ruler and parent; what ruler and parent bind is loyalty and filial piety alone.
translations.idiomatic: Nothing outweighs sovereign and father; both demand loyalty and filial piety.

sentences.zh: 孝以揚親為主，忠以節義為先。

translations.literal: Filial piety takes exalting parents as lord; loyalty takes integrity as foremost.
translations.idiomatic: Filial piety honors parents; loyalty demands moral courage.

sentences.zh: 殷侯忠貞居正，心貫人神，加與先帝隆布衣之好，著莫逆之契，契闊艱難，夷嶮以之，雖受屈奸雄，志達千載，此忠貞之徒所以義幹其心不獲以已者也。

translations.literal: Lord Yin held loyal steadfastness and upright conduct; his mind pierced men and spirits; added to that he had with the late emperor a friendship of plain-cloth intimacy and a covenant of never-breaking trust; through hardship and separation he crossed peril with him; although he suffered insult from a treacherous hero, his aim reached a thousand years—this is why men of loyal steadfastness, righteousness stirring their hearts, could not help themselves.
translations.idiomatic: Yin Hao’s loyalty and his bond with the late emperor are legend—patriots cannot forget him.

sentences.zh: 既當時貞烈之徒所究見，亦後生所備聞，吾亦何敢苟避狂狡，以欺聖明。

translations.literal: It is what the chaste and heroic of that age investigated and saw, and what later-born men have fully heard—how dare I evade mad treachery to deceive sagely brightness!
translations.idiomatic: All honest men know his story; I will not lie to the throne.

sentences.zh: 足下不推居正之大致，而懷知己之小惠，欲以幕府之小節奪名教之重義，於君臣之階既以虧矣。

translations.literal: You do not promote the great drift of upright conduct but harbor the small kindness of personal knowledge, wishing to use the minor points of a staff headquarters to wrest the weighty righteousness of name-teaching—in the steps of ruler and minister this is already deficient.
translations.idiomatic: You prize private patronage over public ethics—you fail both ruler and minister.

sentences.zh: 尊大君以殷侯協契忠規，同戴王室，志厲秋霜，誠貫一時，殷侯所以得宣其義聲，實尊大君協贊之力也。

translations.literal: Your honored father, because Lord Yin joined in loyal counsel and together supported the royal house, his resolve sharpened like autumn frost, his sincerity piercing the age—this is the reason Lord Yin could broadcast his righteous fame, truly the force of your honored father’s coordinated aid.
translations.idiomatic: Your father and Yin Hao together served the Jin—Yin’s voice lived because your father backed him.

sentences.zh: 足下不能光大君此之直志，乃感溫小顧，懷其曲澤，公在聖世，欺罔天下，使丞相之德不及三葉，領軍之基一構而傾，此忠臣所以解心，孝子所以喪氣，父子之道固若是乎？

translations.literal: You cannot enlarge your honored father’s straight resolve of this kind, yet you feel Huan Wen’s small favor, cherish his crooked kindness—while the duke is in a sagely age you deceive the realm, making the chancellor’s virtue not reach three generations, making the foundation of the commander of the guards topple at one stroke—is this how the way of father and son truly is?
translations.idiomatic: You betray your father’s alliance with Yin for Huan Wen’s favors—you shame your house and the state.

sentences.zh: 足下言臣則非忠，語子則非孝。

translations.literal: What you say as a subject is not loyal; what you speak as a son is not filial.
translations.idiomatic: As minister you are disloyal; as son unfilial.

sentences.zh: 二者既亡，吾誰畏哉！

translations.literal: When both are lost, whom do I fear!
translations.idiomatic: With neither virtue left, I fear no one.

sentences.zh: 吾少嘗過庭，備聞祖考之言，未嘗不發憤沖冠，情見乎辭。

translations.literal: In youth I once passed the courtyard and fully heard the words of grandfathers and deceased father; never did I fail to bristle with rage till my cap rose; the feeling showed in the phrasing.
translations.idiomatic: I grew up hearing elders curse Huan Wen’s crimes.

sentences.zh: 當爾之時，惟覆亡是懼，豈暇謀及國家。

translations.literal: In that moment I feared only ruin and destruction—how had I leisure to scheme for the state.
translations.idiomatic: Then I thought only of survival, not policy.

sentences.zh: 不圖今日得操筆斯事，是以上憤國朝無正義之臣，次惟祖考有沒身之恨，豈得與足下同其肝膽邪！

translations.literal: I did not expect today to grasp the brush on this affair—therefore above I resent that the court lacks ministers of righteous principle, below I think of grandfathers and father with hatred unto death—how can I share liver and gall with you!
translations.idiomatic: Now I write because the court lacks justice and my family died unavenged—I am no ally of yours.

sentences.zh: 先君往亦嘗為其吏，于時危懼，恆不自保，仰首聖朝，心口憤歎，豈復得計策名昔日，自同在三邪！

translations.literal: My late father once likewise was his clerk; at that time peril and fear were constant, he could not preserve himself; looking up to the sagely court, heart and mouth burned with resentment—how could he compare to inscribing his name in earlier days and counting himself among those bound by the three!
translations.idiomatic: My father served Huan Wen in terror—do not equate him with willing clients.

sentences.zh: 昔子政以五世純臣，子駿以下委質王莽，先典既已正其逆順，後人亦已鑒其成敗。

translations.literal: Long ago Liu Xiang, through five generations a pure minister, yet Liu Xin below him submitted his substance to Wang Mang—the former canon already rectified their rebellion and submission, later men have also mirrored their success and failure.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xiang’s purity did not stop Liu Xin from serving Wang Mang—history judges both.

sentences.zh: 每讀其事，未嘗不臨文痛歎，憤愾交懷。

translations.literal: Whenever I read their affair, never do I fail to face the text with pained sigh, indignation and grief crossing in my breast.
translations.idiomatic: Each reading wrings my heart.

sentences.zh: 以今況古，乃知一揆耳。

translations.literal: Comparing today with antiquity, then one knows it is a single pattern.
translations.idiomatic: Past and present follow the same pattern.

sentences.zh: 弘之詞雖亮直，終以桓、謝之故不調，卒于餘杭令，年四十七。

translations.literal: Although Hongzhi’s language was bright and straight, in the end because of the Huan and Xie affair he was not transferred [upward], and died as magistrate of Yuhang, aged forty-seven.
translations.idiomatic: His candor cost him promotion; he died Yuhang magistrate at forty-seven, a victim of Huan and Xie politics.

sentences.zh: 王歡

translations.literal: Wang Huan
translations.idiomatic: Wang Huan

sentences.zh: 王歡，字君厚，樂陵人也。

translations.literal: Wang Huan, styled Junhou, was a man of Leling.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Huan, courtesy Junhou, came from Leling.

sentences.zh: 安貧樂道，專精耽學，不營產業，常丐食誦《詩》，雖家無斗儲，意怡如也。

translations.literal: Content with poverty and devoted to the Way, he concentrated essence and delighted in learning, did not manage property, often begged food while reciting the Poetry; although his house lacked a peck in storage, his mind was cheerful as ever.
translations.idiomatic: He embraced poverty for learning, begged meals while chanting the Odes, and stayed cheerful though his granary was empty.

sentences.zh: 其妻患之，或焚毀其書而求改嫁，歡笑而謂之曰：「卿不聞朱買臣妻邪？

translations.literal: His wife worried over this; once she burned his books and sought to remarry; Huan laughed and said to her, "Have you not heard of Zhu Maichen’s wife?"
translations.idiomatic: His wife burned his books to force divorce; he cited Zhu Maichen’s foolish wife.

sentences.zh: 」時聞者多哂之。

translations.literal: Those who heard at the time mostly sneered at him.
translations.idiomatic: Listeners mostly sneered.

sentences.zh: 歡守志彌固，遂為通儒。

translations.literal: Huan kept his resolve all the firmer and thereupon became a thoroughly learned Ru.
translations.idiomatic: He held his course and became a master scholar.

sentences.zh: 至慕容晞襲偽號，署為國子博士，親就受經。

translations.literal: When Murong Xi assumed a usurped title, he appointed him erudite of the imperial academy and personally came to receive instruction in the classics.
translations.idiomatic: Murong Xi made him academy erudite and attended his lectures in person.

sentences.zh: 遷祭酒。

translations.literal: He was promoted libationer.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to libationer.

sentences.zh: 及晞為苻堅所滅，歡死于長安。

translations.literal: When Xi was destroyed by Fu Jian, Huan died in Chang’an.
translations.idiomatic: When Fu Jian overthrew Murong Xi, Wang Huan died in Chang’an.

sentences.zh: 史評

translations.literal: Historian’s appraisal
translations.idiomatic: Historian’s appraisal

sentences.zh: 史臣曰：范平等學府儒宗，譽隆望重，或質疑是屬，或師範攸歸，雖為未及古人，故亦一時之俊。

translations.literal: The historians say: Fan Ping and the like were patriarchs of the academies, their fame lofty and weight heavy; some belonged to those who raised doubts, some were where models returned; although they did not reach the ancients, still they were fine men of their age.
translations.idiomatic: The historians: men like Fan Ping led the scholarly world—though not ancient sages, they were luminaries of their day.

sentences.zh: 若仲寧之清貞守道，抗志柴門；

translations.literal: Such as Zhongning’s pure chastity in guarding the Way, resisting ambition at a brushwood gate;
translations.idiomatic: Yu Xi’s spotless reclusion;

sentences.zh: 行齊之居室屢空，棲心陋巷；

translations.literal: Xingqi’s dwelling repeatedly empty, mind roosting in a mean lane;
translations.idiomatic: Du Yi’s bare rooms and humble lane;

sentences.zh: 文博之漱流枕石，鏟跡銷聲；

translations.literal: Wenbo’s rinsing in streams and pillowing on stones, scraping tracks and silencing fame;
translations.idiomatic: Dong Jingdao’s stream-side hermitage;

sentences.zh: 宣子之樂道安貧，弘風闡教：斯並通儒之高尚者也。

translations.literal: Xuanzi’s delight in the Way and contentment with poverty, spreading the wind and clarifying teaching: these together were the high-mindedness of thorough Ru.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Xuan’s joyful poverty and teaching—all were noble Confucian lives.

sentences.zh: 而邈協和主相，刊削繁辭，可謂將順其美，匡救其惡。

translations.literal: Yet Miao harmonized ruler and minister, cutting and revising redundant phrasing—this may be called following what was beautiful in them and remedying what was evil.
translations.idiomatic: Xu Miao reconciled sovereign and regent and edited the emperor’s words—amplifying good, curbing harm.

sentences.zh: 舒元入參機務，明主賞其博聞；

translations.literal: Shuyuan entered to participate in the subtle tasks, and the enlightened ruler prized his broad hearing;
translations.idiomatic: Kong Yan advised on statecraft and won the ruler’s esteem for his learning;

sentences.zh: 出蒞邊隅，獷狄欽其明德。

translations.literal: going out to govern a border corner, the wild Di admired his bright virtue.
translations.idiomatic: posted to the frontier, he impressed even barbarians with his character.

sentences.zh: 弘之抗言立論，不避朝權，貶石抵溫，斯為當矣，遂乃厄三怨，以至陵遲，悲夫！

translations.literal: Hongzhi raised his voice and framed disputation, not avoiding court power, demoting Shi and striking at Wen—this was fitting; yet thereupon he met three resentments, until he sank into decline—how sad!
translations.idiomatic: Fan Hongzhi spoke truth to power, indicting Xie Shi and Huan Wen rightly, yet three grudges ruined him—pitiful!

sentences.zh: 贊曰：鬱鬱周文，洋洋漢典。

translations.literal: The encomium says: Luxuriant was Zhou’s pattern, vast Han’s canon.
translations.idiomatic: Encomium: Zhou’s culture flourished, Han’s canon flowed wide;

sentences.zh: 炙輠流譽，解頤飛辯。

translations.literal: Roasted skewers spread reputation, loosened jaws flew in disputation.
translations.idiomatic: wit won fame, eloquence soared;

sentences.zh: 雅誥弗淪，微言復顯。

translations.literal: Elegant admonitions were not lost, subtle words shone again.
translations.idiomatic: great instructions endured, subtle teachings returned;

sentences.zh: 爰及晉代，斯風逾闡。

translations.literal: Reaching to the Jin age, this wind was further clarified.
translations.idiomatic: under Jin that spirit burned brighter still.
